title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes
length: Introduction + 4 parts, 47 chapters + a Review and Conclusion (49 reading units)
openingText: Nature (the art by which God has made and governs the world) is imitated by the art of man in many things, and in this one too: that human art can make an Artificial Animal. For since life is but a motion of limbs, beginning in some principal part within, why may we not say that all Automata have an artificial life? For what is the heart but a spring; the nerves but so many strings; the joints but so many wheels.
about:
Hobbes wrote Leviathan in Paris while England was in the middle of the civil war that beheaded its king. He had fled the country with the royalists in 1640 and was tutoring the future Charles II when the book appeared in 1651. The argument is austere and consecutive. Hobbes begins with the smallest unit — a single mind perceiving the world — and works outward, by definitions and deductions, to the largest unit: the artificial body of the state. The first part, 'Of Man,' is a theory of human nature: sensation, imagination, language, reason, the passions, religion, and what life looks like in the absence of any common authority — the famous 'natural condition of mankind,' which Hobbes describes as a state of war of every man against every man, and human life in it as 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.'

The second part, 'Of Commonwealth,' is the constructive argument. To escape the state of nature, men contract with one another to give up their natural right to act on their own judgement and transfer that right to a single sovereign — one man or one assembly — whose word is law. The sovereign is not a party to the contract; the contract is among the subjects themselves to obey whatever the sovereign commands. Hobbes argues from this premise that the sovereign's authority must be absolute and undivided, that there is no right of resistance except where the sovereign fails to protect the subject's life, and that the only check on sovereign power is the moral pressure of the law of nature acting on the sovereign's own conscience.

Parts III and IV apply the same logic to religion and to political theology. Hobbes is determined to leave no scriptural authority outside the civil sovereign; he rereads the Bible, redefines 'the kingdom of God,' and dismantles what he calls the Roman Catholic Church's claim to a temporal jurisdiction independent of the state. The book ends with a Review and Conclusion in which Hobbes adds one more law of nature — that every man is bound to protect the authority that protects him — and defends the whole discourse against the charge of impiety. Leviathan has been the central text of modern political philosophy ever since, the founding work of the social-contract tradition and the most uncompromising case ever made for sovereign authority as the precondition of any tolerable life.

angleCards.title: The state of nature.
angleCards.text: Hobbes's central thought experiment: if there were no common power to keep men in awe, what would life be like? His answer — war of every man against every man, life solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short — is the foundation of everything that follows.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Hobbes's argument for the state of nature in Chapter 13 — what he claims about human equality, scarcity, and fear — and decide whether his account of life without a sovereign is convincing.

angleCards.title: The covenant.
angleCards.text: Chapters 14–17 build the social contract. Men agree, each with each, to surrender their natural right to act on their own judgement and transfer it to a single sovereign whose word is law. The contract is among the subjects; the sovereign is not a party to it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the covenant chapters carefully — what Hobbes thinks the parties are agreeing to, what the sovereign is and is not bound by, and what kind of obligation results.

angleCards.title: Absolute sovereignty.
angleCards.text: Part II argues that sovereign power, once instituted, must be absolute and undivided. No right of resistance except where the sovereign fails to protect life. No separation of powers. Read Hobbes's reasons and test them against everything you know about politics since.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Hobbes's case for absolute sovereignty on its own terms — and then weigh it against the constitutional, separation-of-powers tradition that comes after him.

angleCards.title: Religion and the kingdom of darkness.
angleCards.text: Parts III and IV are about church and state. Hobbes rereads scripture to leave every religious authority subordinate to the civil sovereign, and gives the Roman Catholic Church the title 'Kingdom of Darkness.' Modern readers tend to skip these parts. Skip them and you miss what the book is for.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the religious chapters of Leviathan — the reinterpretation of scripture and the polemic against the 'Kingdom of Darkness' — and understand why Hobbes thought the political argument was incomplete without them.

cast.name: The Sovereign
cast.description: Not a person but an office. The Sovereign is whoever — one man or one assembly — holds, by the covenant of the subjects, the undivided right to make laws, judge, punish, and decide on war and peace. Hobbes's whole argument is that this office must be created and that, once created, it cannot be limited without dissolving the state that depends on it.

cast.name: The Subject
cast.description: Every subject is bound by the covenant they have made with every other subject to obey the sovereign in all things the sovereign commands, except where the command would directly destroy the subject's own life. Hobbes's idea of obligation is symmetrical: the subject owes obedience for protection, and only for protection. When protection fails, so does the duty to obey.

cast.name: Natural Man
cast.description: The human being before the state, equipped with senses, passions, reason, and a natural right to do whatever he judges necessary for his own preservation. In Part I Hobbes builds him up from physiology and language. In Chapter 13 he places him in the state of nature, where the natural right and the natural condition collide and life becomes intolerable.

cast.name: The Commonwealth
cast.description: Hobbes calls the state 'a Mortal God,' an artificial person built out of the contracts of all its subjects. The opening pages compare it to a giant body — sovereignty its soul, magistrates its joints, wealth its strength, laws its reason, sedition its sickness, civil war its death. The frontispiece of the 1651 edition shows it as a crowned giant made of small human figures.

cast.name: The Church
cast.description: Parts III and IV are Hobbes's argument against any ecclesiastical power independent of the civil sovereign. The Bible itself, he insists, is sovereign only in the form the civil power has authorised. The Roman Catholic Church, in particular, gets the title of 'Kingdom of Darkness' — an authority that uses fear of the next world to extract obedience from this one, and that Hobbes regards as the chief rival to the peace of any commonwealth.

cast.name: Thomas Hobbes
cast.description: An English philosopher (1588–1679), tutor to William Cavendish and later to the future Charles II, friend of Galileo and of the French mathematicians around Mersenne. He wrote Leviathan in Paris in exile from a country in civil war, intending it both as theory and as practical advice. Hobbes was the first major modern philosopher to ground politics on a materialist account of human nature, and he was attacked from every direction for it for the rest of his life.

acclaim.quote: If I had read Hobbes, I had been completely undone.
acclaim.source: John Aubrey, recording Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon
acclaim.context: Aubrey's Brief Lives, on Clarendon's reaction to first reading Leviathan, written 1670s

acclaim.quote: Modern political philosophy begins with Hobbes.
acclaim.context: The Political Philosophy of Hobbes: Its Basis and Its Genesis, Oxford, 1936

acclaim.quote: Hobbes was the greatest of English political philosophers.

whyItMatters.title: The Sentence Everyone Knows
whyItMatters.body: In Chapter 13, after a page and a half of dry argument about how rough natural equality combines with scarcity to produce competition, diffidence, and the pursuit of glory, Hobbes hands his reader the single most quoted sentence in political philosophy. In the state of nature, he writes, 'there is no place for industry, because the fruit thereof is uncertain; and consequently no culture of the earth; no navigation, nor use of the commodities that may be imported by sea; no commodious building; no instruments of moving and removing such things as require much force; no knowledge of the face of the earth; no account of time; no arts; no letters; no society; and which is worst of all, continual fear, and danger of violent death; and the life of man, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.' The list has the rhythm of a hammer. It is the picture every later social-contract thinker has had to refute or accommodate, and the dark mirror against which Locke, Rousseau, and Rawls all wrote. It is also, on Hobbes's own terms, an argument from inside the reader: not a historical claim about what once was, but a deduction about what would be the moment the common power lapsed. Modern political philosophy, in the sense in which it differs from ancient, begins with this paragraph.

whyItMatters.title: The Most Uncompromising Argument for Sovereignty
whyItMatters.body: Almost everyone who comes to Leviathan comes wanting to find a way around its central conclusion. Hobbes makes that hard. He argues, step by step, that the sovereign's authority cannot be divided (because divided sovereignty is the same as no sovereignty), that it cannot be limited by law (because the sovereign makes the laws), that it cannot be checked by a constituent power (because the subjects have already given up the right to constitute), and that there is no right of resistance except to a direct order to die. He concedes only one point: a subject may not be obliged to do something that defeats the purpose for which sovereignty was instituted — namely, the preservation of the subject's life. Everything else is the sovereign's. This is the position later constitutional thought spent three centuries trying to refute. The arguments worth reading against it — Locke, Spinoza, Rousseau, Hegel, Schmitt, Rawls — are all visibly engaged with Hobbes's text. The reader who has not actually walked through Hobbes's argument is not yet in the conversation.

whyItMatters.title: Religion Is Not a Sidebar
whyItMatters.body: Modern editions of Leviathan often advertise Parts I and II as the philosophical core and treat Parts III and IV — 'Of a Christian Commonwealth' and 'Of the Kingdom of Darkness' — as a religious appendix that can be skipped. Hobbes did not write the book that way. Parts III and IV are nearly half the text, and they are where the political argument lands. Hobbes rereads scripture to show that the Israelites' commonwealth was a sovereign state with God as its sovereign, that the New Testament does not establish a separate ecclesiastical authority, and that any priesthood claiming jurisdiction over the conscience of subjects independent of the civil power is, in his term, a 'Kingdom of Darkness.' The Roman Catholic Church is the named target, but the argument cuts at any religious community that claims to bind subjects beyond what the sovereign permits. This is the part of Leviathan that produced the seventeenth-century scandal, the part that was banned in Oxford and burned in some places, and the part without which the political argument has no edge. Hobbes wrote the political theory because he wanted to settle the religious question. The reader who skips Parts III and IV reads the prelude and not the case.
